results.summary:
Connecting mesh Wi-Fi satellite nodes to a primary router via Ethernet cables, known as wired backhaul, significantly improves network speeds by eliminating common wireless signal performance penalties.

### Key Points
- Wireless backhaul in mesh systems often causes a 50% speed reduction because nodes operate in half-duplex mode, alternating between sending and receiving data.
- Wired backhaul uses Ethernet cables to link satellite nodes directly to the main router, bypassing the interference and signal loss inherent in wireless connections.
- Users can implement wired backhaul by connecting nodes to an unmanaged switch, such as the Netgear 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet switch, to maintain full network management.
- Testing with a Google Nest Wi-Fi Pro system showed that switching from wireless to wired backhaul increased speeds from half of the network's capacity to over 900Mbps.
- While wired backhaul offers superior performance, it requires the physical installation of Ethernet cables, which may be challenging for users without existing home networking infrastructure.

### Why it Matters
Transitioning to a wired backhaul configuration allows users to maximize the performance of their mesh networking hardware by removing the inherent limitations of wireless signal hops. This approach provides a reliable, high-speed connection that is essential for bandwidth-intensive tasks like gaming and streaming, even in homes with large floor plans.

results.title: PCI SSC calls for human approval of AI agent actions involving cardholder data
results.author: Anamarija Pogorelec
results.content:
PCI SSC calls for human approval of AI agent actions involving cardholder data
The PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC) has published Security Considerations for AI Systems, guidance covering the protection of data supplied to AI systems in payment environments and defenses against AI-assisted attacks.
Developed with industry stakeholders, the document addresses governance, deployment, access controls, testing and the application of PCI standards. Its recommendations are advisory, and existing PCI requirements take precedence.
“As AI is increasingly used in payment environments, there is an obligation for all parties to ensure the technology is used responsibly,” said Gina Gobeyn, Executive Director, PCI SSC. “This additional guidance provides a practical starting point for secure AI implementation.”
PCI DSS scoping for AI systems (Source: PCI SSC)
Define access and accountability
The Council recommends defining an AI system’s purpose, permissions and data access before selecting or deploying it. Its least agency approach limits each system to the access and capabilities needed for its assigned tasks.
A suitable human individual should formally accept responsibility for AI output, and organizations should specify which actions require human approval. Access restrictions should be enforced through independent controls, such as identity-management policies and network isolation.
Organizations should avoid combining sensitive data access, external communications and unrestricted input from untrusted sources in one AI system. Where a workflow needs all three, the guidance recommends separating responsibilities among agents with different permissions.
An AI inventory and bill of materials should identify models, versions, hosting, integrations, data-use and retention policies, and intended users. An acceptable-use policy and technical controls should help identify and restrict shadow AI, tools employees deploy or use without approval.
Test controls and prepare for failure
Safeguards should be tested before extensive functional or user-acceptance testing. This includes adversarial testing to determine whether restrictions can be bypassed.
Monitoring and revalidation should continue throughout deployment to detect changes in behavior. Review processes should also account for excessive trust in AI output, which can cause reviewers to overlook mistakes.
The guidance describes human approval for each task and an alternative in which AI systems perform authorized actions under monitoring without approval for every individual action. For monitored autonomy, organizations should define permitted actions, approval requirements, shutdown triggers and procedures for reversing changes. A suitable human individual should remain ultimately responsible.
For agents with access to cleartext cardholder data, explicit human approval for any actions involving that data is recommended.
Protect sensitive data and credentials
AI systems should not handle, generate or manage unprotected high-impact secrets, including passwords and cryptographic keys. Credentials should be managed through secrets-management tools and kept out of source code, prompts, AI context, outputs and logs.
When random values are required, the Council recommends using a trusted random-number generator. Values used for passwords or cryptographic keys may need to remain outside the AI system.
Organizations should use encrypted or tokenized payment data where possible. Data-loss prevention controls should operate independently of the AI, and logs should support investigations without retaining sensitive payment information.
PCI scoping should consider an AI system’s deployment, isolation, access to account data, including data used for training, and ability to affect the security of cardholder-data systems. Access to encrypted or tokenized data together with tools that decrypt or detokenize it should be treated as access to readable data.
Address AI-assisted attacks
The Council warns that AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery, exploit development and social engineering. It recommends ongoing vulnerability monitoring and a process for prioritizing findings and patches.
Defenses include limiting services and permissions, isolating legacy systems, using phishing-resistant authentication, encrypting sensitive data and containing the impact of breaches.
AI-generated code and patches should undergo security and functional testing. Reviews should check for embedded credentials, unsuitable dependencies, newly introduced weaknesses and whether fixes address the underlying problem.
One deployment example divides vulnerability management among agents that identify issues, prepare patching plans, test changes and deploy approved updates. Permissions are assigned by role, and rollback procedures are tested before deployment.
Assess external providers
External AI providers with access to sensitive data should be assessed under applicable third-party service provider requirements. Agreements should address responsibility for sensitive information, explicitly prohibit using the organization’s data for AI training, provide visibility into subcontractors and set breach notification terms.
Incident response plans and periodic testing should cover prompt injection, model poisoning, actions outside approved scope and unauthorized AI tools accessing sensitive data.
results.summary:
The PCI Security Standards Council has released new guidance requiring human oversight for AI agents handling cardholder data to mitigate security risks and prevent unauthorized system access.

### Key Points
- The PCI SSC recommends that human operators provide explicit approval for any AI actions involving cleartext cardholder data.
- Organizations should implement a "least agency" approach, limiting AI system permissions to only the specific capabilities required for assigned tasks.
- The guidance advises maintaining an AI inventory and bill of materials to track models, data-use policies, and unauthorized "shadow AI" tools.
- Security teams should conduct adversarial testing to identify potential vulnerabilities and ensure AI systems cannot bypass established access controls.
- Sensitive credentials, such as cryptographic keys and passwords, must be managed through independent tools rather than being stored in AI prompts or logs.
- Third-party AI providers must be assessed for compliance, with contracts explicitly prohibiting the use of company data for model training.

### Why it Matters
This guidance provides a critical framework for businesses integrating AI into payment environments where data security is paramount. By mandating human accountability and strict access controls, the PCI SSC aims to reduce the risk of automated breaches and ensure that AI adoption does not compromise existing payment security standards.

results.title: A New Mexico Community Was a Place to Build a Life. Then a Hypersonic Missile Factory Showed Up
results.author: Yulia Almazova
results.content:
Sally Schultz thought she had struck gold when she purchased land in Rio Rancho Estates, an unincorporated, census-designated community just outside the city of Rio Rancho, New Mexico. A single mother of four, Schultz came there following a divorce to build a homestead of her own and finally gain some stability in her life.
For $3,500, she was able to purchase half an acre for her trailer in a rural area located close to numerous elementary schools and parks. In a relatively short time, she was able to coax crops like corn, squash, and green chile from the ground. This cheap land became Schultz’s haven, giving her a second chance at life.
Then a missile company showed up next door.
“We’ve already been through so much,” she says, “and now we have to leave. It is the unknowing that is scariest.”
Castelion, a startup founded in November 2022 by three former SpaceX executives, is building Project Ranger, which it claims will be America’s “largest dedicated hypersonic manufacturing production facility.” Construction is set to be complete by the end of the year.
The company’s chosen site for its mega-campus is, in some cases, it appears, a little more than 1,000 yards away from roughly 450 properties in Rio Rancho Estates, including Schultz’s. That puts the homes squarely within a danger zone should any explosive chemicals stored onsite catch fire.
A year into Castelion’s relationship with the state of New Mexico, the company—which declined to speak with WIRED for this story—still hasn’t answered basic safety questions, even as an official hazard assessment found buildings would simply be left to burn in the case of fire, releasing hydrochloric acid gas into the air. Emails between the company and Rio Rancho officials reviewed by WIRED also show Castelion was negotiating fire safety standards even after construction was well underway.
“I live next door to where World War III will be manufactured,” says local resident Laura Lundberg.
Big Plans
Castelion has become a bit of a darling among the new wave of defense tech startups. The company has recently hit a valuation of $13 billion—more than four times its Series B valuation of $2.8 billion from last year.
It has received over $500 million in US military contracts in just 18 months, swiftly securing its spot as one of the “Arsenal of Freedom” suppliers.
The firm touts its ability to make hypersonic missiles—a label for any missile flying at five times the speed of sound or higher—at a lower cost than its competitors. The US Army’s Dark Eagle is the most mature domestic hypersonic weapon, and it costs an estimated $41 million per missile, according to a 2023 Congressional Budget Office study. Castelion’s main product, Blackbeard, is a solid-rocket-powered missile that was set to sell for $384,000 per unit.
In reality, the missiles are looking as if they will turn out pricier than initially advertised.
Castelion kicked off the year with a nearly $50 million Navy contract to build full-scale prototypes of its Blackbeard missile. By June, the Navy expanded the effort, adding another $23.4 million to supply the first 50 operational Blackbeard prototypes. Then, in August, the Navy doubled down with another $90 million contract to cover manufacturing services for the same 50 Blackbeards—pushing the total to $163.4 million for 50 missiles, or $3.3 million per unit.
And most recently, in September, the Navy awarded Castelion the company’s largest contract yet—up to $200 million.
Recently, Castelion released the first photo of its Blackbeard hypersonic strike missile, but concrete performance figures for Blackbeard remain hidden. Castelion has not publicly released any test data to verify its weapon’s efficacy.
Project Ranger will become Castelion’s biggest manufacturing and testing hub. The company broke ground on the 1,000-acre facility on January 21, and it’s targeting mass production as early as next year.
The facility wasn’t always supposed to be in New Mexico, though.
Unredacted
In August 2023, the company applied to build a rocket factory in Churchill County, Nevada, under a different name—Pallas Industrials. Chief financial officer Andrew Kreitz signed a special use application, which disclosed the company’s plans to build rocket motors and ground-test them up to eight days a month at the site.
In response to the application, Churchill County officials provided eight pages of staff analysis and required the company to provide testing conditions and safety protocols. Not long afterward, Pallas Industrials pulled out of Nevada under the new name: Castelion. A few months later, the company began testing the soil in western Rio Rancho.
Rio Rancho Estates residents say that by the time they started noticing soil-probing trucks in the spring of 2025, Castelion was already in a conversation with New Mexico officials about using the land for the missile factory.
In June 2025, Sandia National Labs delivered a hazard report as part of the New Mexico Small Business Assistance Program, originally intended to help local small businesses access the expertise of Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories at absolutely no cost.
Under the Freedom of Information Act, Sandia later released a heavily redacted version of the report. Instead of scrubbing the underlying data layer of the file, the lab simply put black ink highlight over black text, leaving the full unredacted report accessible via copying and pasting.
The report alleges Castelion’s plans to build and operate the missile factory present significant risks.
It identifies a massive “storage facility fire” as the worst-case scenario. Castelion is set to store colossal stockpiles of propellants on Project Ranger’s site. The company has publicly stated its plans of working with at least one heat-sensitive chemical oxidizer—ammonium perchlorate—and storing up to 250,000 pounds inside covered magazines and bunkers, according to the Sandia report. But outside those bunkers, the report notes, Castelion is allowed to keep up to 81,000 pounds of active explosive material at a time inside the hazardous integration facilities during the assembly process.
A detonation of the facility’s largest allowed stockpile of explosive material would require a buffer from the nearest inhabited building of almost nine football fields in length. Sandia calculated that a worst-case explosion could shatter large windows as far as almost four miles away and have a 3.2 percent chance of causing minor eardrum damage to people 400 yards from the detonation.
Sandia declined to provide comment for WIRED. One of the hazard reports authors, Meg Davidson, has since left Sandia Labs and is now a senior manager of strategic partnerships at Castelion. She did not respond to requests for comment.
The report identifies a fire at the test stand as “the most probable foreseeable hazardous event.” A chemical fire would release a toxic haze containing byproducts like hydrogen chloride and chlorine. In gas form, both are highly corrosive and can cause severe eye, skin, and respiratory tract burns. Even short-term inhalation at high concentrations can cause chemical lung damage and asphyxiation.
Emails obtained through public records requests reveal that the Rio Rancho Fire Department determined 17 of the 26 buildings at the Project Ranger site would be left to burn if a fire ignited, due to the risks a chemical blaze would pose first responders. Firefighters would be barred from even entering the high-risk facilities.
Such events are hardly unheard of. WIRED reported on a June incident at Anduril’s Mississippi facility where a test run of an ammonium perchlorate–based rocket motor ended in an explosion. The blast—which didn’t cause any casualties—underscored the technical risks of scaling solid propellant production.
In May, a storage tank holding approximately 7,000 gallons of methyl methacrylate, a flammable liquid used to manufacture acrylic plastics and resins for military and commercial aircraft, began to overheat at a GKN Aerospace plant in Garden Grove, California, leading local authorities to evacuate more than 40,000 residents.
Despite these warnings, internal emails obtained through public records requests reveal that Castelion was still negotiating critical fire-response requirements between March and May—even as construction had already started.
Castelion’s site developer, Bryce Barlow, wrote to the city on March 23 that the company had not yet finalized the fire-flow response, offering to discuss the question by phone or in person instead.
After a few weeks, the requirements were replaced by city manager Matt Geisel with a statement that hard numbers would appear in the plans later on. Castelion only needed a signed memorandum of understanding to proceed—backed by the governing body’s resolution and a serviceability letter.
“Great news! Saves all of us both legal bills and headaches,” Kreitz wrote in response.
‘A Done Deal’
In August 2025, prior to Castelion’s formal announcement that it had selected New Mexico, Republican state senator Jay Block appeared before the Sandoval County Commission to speak in support of financing Project Ranger. Before becoming state senator, Block was a county commissioner.
The county had approved $125 million in industrial revenue bonds and had passed a resolution giving itself control over the state land picked for the site. The commissioners granted an astounding 95 percent discount on what Castelion would normally owe in property taxes. Finally, the county agreed to abate compensating taxes on out-of-state equipment, lowering the upfront costs for the incoming missile manufacturer to relocate to New Mexico.
Block’s district includes Rio Rancho as of January.
“I strongly supported Project Ranger as it moved through the local approval process, because I believed Rio Rancho and Sandoval County had the workforce, infrastructure, and defense heritage to help Castelion succeed,” Block tells WIRED.
Castelion held its first public information meeting on Project Ranger in October 2025.
“All of this happened behind the scenes. By the time it was public, it was already a done deal,” says Zachary Darden, a Rio Rancho resident who ran an unsuccessful bid for mayor on a platform opposing the development.
In November, emails show Alberto Solís, Rio Rancho’s economic development manager, coordinated Castelion CFO Kreitz’s four-day trip to New Mexico—part of the outreach process required by the state. The CFO asked to attend a Chamber of Commerce “Jingle Mingle” mixer and an event with the Sandoval Economic Alliance, a local nonprofit tasked with recruiting new business to the county.
More than a month after Kreitz’s networking trip, Castelion held its groundbreaking ceremony. Local residents weren’t invited, but many of the state’s most prominent political and business figures were. Block was there as well as US senator Martin Heinrich. So were Gregg Hull, Rio Rancho’s then mayor and Republican candidate for governor, as well as Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. County and state economic development officials were also in attendance.
“Castelion's Project Ranger shows what a strong public-private partnership can deliver for a local community,” Rob Black, New Mexico’s secretary of economic development, tells WIRED.
Residents living next to the site, though, are contemplating whether the risks are too high to stay. But for most living in Rio Rancho Estates—a low-income neighborhood—the costs of relocation might be too high.
“This land is affordable for people who need it,” says community member Jason Clifford. “We were sold out by our local officials.”
results.summary:
Defense startup Castelion is constructing a massive hypersonic missile manufacturing facility in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, sparking safety concerns among residents living near the high-risk production site.

### Key Points
- Castelion’s Project Ranger facility is located within 1,000 yards of approximately 450 homes in the Rio Rancho Estates community.
- A Sandia National Labs hazard report warns that a worst-case explosion could shatter windows four miles away and release toxic hydrochloric acid gas.
- Internal documents reveal that local fire departments determined 17 of the 26 site buildings would be left to burn during a chemical fire due to safety risks.
- The company has secured over $500 million in US military contracts, including a $200 million award for its Blackbeard hypersonic missile.
- Sandoval County granted Castelion a 95 percent property tax discount and $125 million in industrial revenue bonds to facilitate the project.

### Why it Matters
The rapid development of Project Ranger highlights the tension between aggressive defense-sector expansion and the safety of surrounding residential communities. This case underscores the potential for significant public health risks when high-stakes military manufacturing is fast-tracked through local government partnerships with limited transparency.

results.title: FBI Seizes 7 Domains, Disrupts Flax Typhoon Tools Used in Critical Infrastructure Intrusions
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Department of Justice (DoJ) have announced the disruption of malicious tools used by a China-linked advanced persistent threat group known as Flax Typhoon.
To that end, the agencies seized several domains and blocked access to platforms that were used to scan, and in some cases infiltrate, U.S. critical infrastructure. The list of seized domains is as follows -
- c0cc[.]cc
- 98aiblog[.]com
- 98aicai[.]com
- 98aicode[.]com
- outlook3650[.]com
- youtubecard[.]com
- linkedinns[.]net
Flax Typhoon, also tracked as Ethereal Panda and RedJuliett, is associated with Integrity Technology Group, a Beijing-based company that contracts with the Chinese government. It was previously attributed to a botnet called Raptor Train that comprised thousands of compromised small office/home office (SOHO) and IoT devices. It was taken down following a U.S. court-authorized operation in September 2024.
"These state-sponsored hackers continue to aggressively target and access networks and systems throughout the world in an effort to identify and steal files and otherwise exploit victims' vulnerabilities," said U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti for the Western District of Pennsylvania.
Court documents allege that Integrity Tech created and operated an IoT botnet that leveraged a variant of the Mirai malware. According to the FBI, the botnet is said to have used a number of domains, including subdomains of w8510[.]com, for command-and-control (C2), enabling bidirectional communications between the operators and devices in the botnet. The botnet itself was controlled and managed by an application named Sparrow.
A database server hosted on the server ("202.182.109[.]151") contained records for more than 1.2 million infected devices as of June 5, 2024, including over 385,000 unique U.S. victim devices. In all, more than 260,000 devices, including approximately 126,000 U.S. devices, were actively infected as of June 5, 2024.
The botnet made use of a tool called Microscan to facilitate reconnaissance and computer vulnerability scanning, allowing the threat actors to identify targets of interest. The Python-based web tool, originally hosted on "198.13.53[.]226," was accessible via the domain "c0cc[.]cc" as recently as September 9, 2026, according to an FBI affidavit. The tool is believed to have been put to use as early as 2017.
MicroScan features over 1,300 penetration testing scripts to scan websites for specific vulnerabilities, including OpenSSL, Oracle WebLogic, Rejetto, WordPress, Juniper ScreenOS, Jenkins, and Apache Struts. The scanner is complemented by open-source tooling like BBScan, dirsearch, Fscan, ksubdomain, masscan, NMAP, OneForAll, ShuiZe, and wpscan that are used to find vulnerabilities in networks and web-based applications.
Some of the targeted companies include a U.S. power company based in South Carolina, a multi-national Non-Governmental Organization, Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies in the natural gas and power sectors, and two Taiwanese universities.
A second Integrity Tech tool is FishHub, which allegedly enabled the exploitation of computer networks through spear-phishing attacks and the deployment of follow-on payloads. Confirmed victims of FishHub-related activity include 20 Taiwanese universities.
"This malware provided Integrity Tech's clients with unauthorized remote access to the victim network or searched for specific files and sent them to servers controlled by Integrity Tech," the DoJ said.
"Integrity Technology Group provided China-linked threat actors with capabilities used to conduct widespread vulnerability scanning and, in some cases, intrusions targeting U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure," said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI's Cyber Division.
"The PRC relies on contractor and enabling companies to expand the reach and scale of its malicious cyber activity. By exposing and disrupting these enablers, we make it harder for the PRC to target American networks and infrastructure."
In tandem, a joint advisory issued by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from the U.S., the U.K., Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Spain has called out the for-profit company for enabling malicious cyber actors to target organizations worldwide by acquiring or building cyber tools for use and sale and compromising networks.
Since at least mid-January 2021, the threat actors have been observed breaking into victim networks and cloud-based services using Python- and Go-based command line utilities, while also relying on cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks to conduct user credential harvesting.
Besides installing SoftEther VPN software clients on victim devices for persistence, the threat actors have been found to use EBurst, an open-source Python-based brute-force tool, to target accounts in Microsoft 365 Cloud environments, and gain unauthorized access to mailbox data using a command-line utility known as office-cli.
"Malicious cyber actors, enabled by Integrity Tech, are uniquely using AI tools, such as automated scanning, alongside large-scale botnets and manual exploitation techniques to compromise and steal confidential data from companies around the world, including critical sectors," the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said.
The development comes as the U.S. State Department announced rewards of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of Zhang Yu, a Chinese national charged in the U.S. in connection with the 2021 Microsoft Exchange Server attacks.
The activity is tracked under the moniker Silk Typhoon (formerly Hafnium). In April 2026, co-defendant Xu Zewei was extradited to the U.S. from Italy to face charges related to allegedly stealing COVID-19 research from U.S.-based universities, immunologists, and virologists.
results.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice and FBI have disrupted a China-linked botnet operated by Integrity Technology Group that compromised hundreds of thousands of critical infrastructure devices globally.

### Key Points
- The FBI seized multiple domains used by the Flax Typhoon threat group to manage a botnet of over 260,000 compromised IoT and SOHO devices.
- Integrity Technology Group, a Beijing-based contractor, allegedly utilized the "Sparrow" application and "Microscan" tool to conduct large-scale vulnerability scanning and network infiltration.
- Forensic data from June 2024 identified over 385,000 unique U.S. victim devices targeted by the group's command-and-control infrastructure.
- The operation targeted diverse sectors, including U.S. power companies, international airports, and universities, using tools like FishHub for spear-phishing and credential harvesting.
- A joint international advisory from seven nations confirmed the group’s use of automated AI tools and brute-force utilities to exploit Microsoft 365 environments.

### Why it Matters
This operation highlights the growing reliance of state-sponsored actors on private, for-profit contractors to scale malicious cyber activities against global critical infrastructure. By dismantling these commercial enablers, authorities aim to increase the operational costs for foreign intelligence services attempting to infiltrate sensitive Western networks.

results.title: Thin friction and thicker walls
results.author: Seth Godin
results.content:
Civilized culture is based on a thin sort of friction. You don’t yell at the library, act boorish at a restaurant or hassle a minor celebrity at the supermarket. It’s just not done.
The result of these human layers and inferences are cues and norms that add up to a connected, generative society.
Add selfish hustle, AI agents and cheap bots, and the thin friction is insufficient. They can multiply exponentially, care little about being shunned and have no interest in their reputation.
Fake sincerity is now cheap. Interchangeable identities subvert a generations-long tradition of owning your words and your actions.
You’ll miss the thin friction when it’s gone, replaced by taller, thicker walls. You might already be noticing it.
Interactivity and permeability to those we don’t know well were largely overlooked foundations in the creation of learning, science and culture. We figured out a scalable approach to “knock knock, who’s there” but now it’s going away.
You won’t be able to knock unless you’re invited first. Of course, the invitation will probably be filtered out.
results.summary:
The proliferation of AI agents and automated bots is eroding the social norms and interpersonal friction that have historically supported human connection, cultural exchange, and public discourse.

### Key Points
- Automated bots and AI agents are increasingly capable of generating high volumes of content without regard for social reputation or community standards.
- The decline of traditional social friction threatens the open, permeable interactions that have long served as foundations for scientific and cultural progress.
- Digital environments are shifting toward restricted access models where users must be pre-verified or invited to participate in online spaces.
- The rise of interchangeable digital identities makes it difficult to distinguish between authentic human communication and synthetic, automated interactions.

### Why it Matters
The erosion of these social norms suggests a future where digital spaces become increasingly siloed and inaccessible to the general public. This shift could fundamentally limit the collaborative potential of the internet by replacing open discourse with gated, filtered environments.

results.title: Is AI the new China Shock?
results.author: Jared Franz
results.content:
When China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, that one move set off the largest capital spending boom the world had ever seen. Investments in factories, machinery, housing and other long-term assets rose from roughly $360 billion in 2000 to $3.2 trillion by 2010. Adjusted for inflation, cumulative Chinese fixed investment over that decade totaled about $20 trillion. In the process, China reshaped global trade, commodities, inflation, labor markets and politics for a generation.
Today, another investment surge of comparable magnitude is underway, but most people are still assuming it’s a technology sector story. They shouldn’t. The artificial intelligence buildout now rivals China’s post-WTO investment boom in scale, and its consequences will extend far beyond the tech sector.
The numbers are staggering. U.S. hyperscalers alone — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet Meta and Oracle — are projected to shell out roughly $800 billion of capital expenditures in 2026, an 83% increase year over year. Research firm Gartner estimates global AI spending will surpass $2 trillion this year. For hard AI capital investment — chips, data centers, power, cooling and networking — estimates cluster around $10 trillion to $15 trillion globally over the next decade. For broader AI spending, including software, services and AI-enabled products, the 10-year total could approach $30 trillion. AI is already China-scale on a hard-capex basis. Under the broader definition, it could be significantly larger than China’s entire 2000–2010 investment surge.
Of course, there are significant differences between the AI and China booms. China produced a physical investment, manufacturing, trade and labor-supply shock. AI is a compute, power, software and cognitive labor shock. But the scale rhymes, and that is what matters for investors, policymakers and anyone trying to understand the macroeconomic landscape as it develops over the next decade. It’s also important to note that China’s story isn’t over. These days, it has continued to move into higher-value industries, including auto manufacturing and health care, along with the development of cheaper AI models that are, by some estimates, only about 5% behind the cutting-edge U.S. models.
Here’s another interesting parallel: China’s manufacturing buildout lowered the cost of physical goods worldwide, unleashing disinflationary forces that suppressed interest rates and compressed manufacturing margins in developed economies. AI is doing something similar through a different channel: lowering the cost of cognitive work. Every task that involves pattern recognition, language processing or data synthesis is now subject to the same deflationary pressure that Chinese manufacturing brought to physical goods two decades ago.
AI’s physical footprint is real, too. The International Energy Agency projects that global data center electricity use will more than double by 2030, reaching 945 terawatt hours, which is roughly equivalent to Japan’s entire current power consumption.
There are a few other critical differences, and they cut both ways. China’s fixed asset investment reached roughly 50% of GDP at its peak, fueled by state-subsidized capital. AI investment, while enormous in absolute terms, is still perhaps 2% of global GDP and driven overwhelmingly by market forces. That may mean AI diffuses faster, since it does not depend on the physical relocation of hundreds of millions of people. China’s shock involved the urbanization of roughly 15% of the world’s population. AI’s shock is global from day one.
The political economy risks may be even more acute. The China shock accelerated inequality and contributed to the political polarization that many democracies are still living with today. AI could turbocharge that dynamic. If it functions primarily as a substitute for cognitive labor rather than a complement, the distributional consequences could be severe. Historian Will Durant argued that inequality tends to be resolved in one of two ways: enlightened redistribution or capital destruction. Neither path is comfortable.
Early labor market data already hints at differentiation. In the U.S., job categories with high exposure to AI are deteriorating faster than low-exposure categories on the order of a quarter of a percentage point per month. And this trend appears to be accelerating.
The bottom line is, the AI debate should not be framed as a tech-sector cycle or a question about whether Nvidia’s valuation is justified. The numbers suggest AI may constitute a macro investment regime, large enough to matter for GDP growth, power demand, capital allocation, labor markets and asset prices across every sector.
We have seen this before. The China shock gave way to new industries and enormous wealth creation. But it also left behind displaced workers, hollowed-out communities, and a populist backlash that took two decades to materialize. That doesn’t mean all investment booms result in similarly difficult circumstances, but it might mean that their second- and third-order effects can define an era. AI’s investment boom is now large enough to be that kind of story. Whether we manage the transition better this time is the defining economic question of the next decade.
Jared Franz is an economist with Capital Group, a Los Angeles-based investment firm with $3.6 trillion in assets under management. He holds a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Chicago and a bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Northwestern University.
The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.
results.summary:
The massive global investment surge in artificial intelligence now rivals China’s post-2001 capital spending boom, signaling a transformative macroeconomic shift that will impact labor markets and global industries.

### Key Points
- U.S. hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet are projected to spend approximately $800 billion on capital expenditures in 2026.
- Global AI-related capital investment for hardware like chips and data centers is estimated to reach $10 trillion to $15 trillion over the next decade.
- The International Energy Agency forecasts that global data center electricity consumption will double by 2030, reaching 945 terawatt hours.
- Unlike China’s manufacturing-led boom, the AI surge is driven by market forces and focuses on compute, software, and cognitive labor efficiency.
- Early U.S. labor data indicates that job categories with high AI exposure are experiencing faster deterioration compared to low-exposure sectors.

### Why it Matters
This investment cycle represents a fundamental macroeconomic regime change that extends far beyond the technology sector to influence global GDP, power demand, and asset prices. Policymakers and investors must prepare for significant societal shifts, as the transition risks mirroring the political and economic polarization that followed the previous era of global industrial expansion.

results.title: ‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
results.author: Stephen Quillen
results.content:
The United States government has moved to exclude some of the world’s top tech companies from a programme that allows them to sponsor skilled foreign workers for permanent residency.
Vice President JD Vance said the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of US workers.
It comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration continues efforts to clamp down on immigration – both legal and undocumented – and make it harder for immigrants to get residency or citizenship.
But the latest move also potentially impacts thousands of foreign workers, many of whom have spent years waiting for a backlog in applications to clear.
Here’s what to know about the latest policy:
How does the current system work?
The suspension concerns the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, which enables a US-based employer to sponsor a foreign worker’s green card — as the permanent residency is commonly known. To qualify, the employer is supposed to demonstrate that there are insufficient US workers for a needed job role and that bringing a foreign worker will not impact the pay or conditions of US workers in the industry.
PERM is a key step in the green card process for many skilled foreign workers. Major tech companies often hire workers on temporary visas, such as the H-1B, before they transition to permanent residency through the PERM process.
What have Vance and others said?
Vance on Thursday accused major companies of fraudulently using the current visa regime to displace US employees and bring in lower-paid foreign workers who amount to “indentured servants”.
“The programme has become rife with fraud,” said Vance at a White House news conference. He claimed that many workers who start off on temporary H-1B visas and later apply for permanent residency under the PERM programme are “being mistreated by their employers” and “used to undercut the wages of American workers”.
“You’ve got to hire great American workers,” the US vice president said. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling used similar language, saying the US would “shut down the pipeline of systemic fraud that has flooded our country”.
“The fraud doesn’t end with getting the job,” said Sonderling. “That job becomes a pathway for foreign workers and their families to stay in America permanently and eventually (become) US citizens.”
“And who pays for it all? The American worker,” he said.
Which companies are impacted?
Vance singled out Microsoft as a major offender and said it would be suspended from the PERM programme.
Other companies whose PERM applications will no longer be processed include US software firm Adobe and some of the world’s top IT firms, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Of these, Capgemini is French, Microsoft and Adobe are American, and the rest — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL — are all Indian.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” said Sonderling.
Vance said the suspensions would continue “as long as it needs to”.
Other companies that rely heavily on H-1B visas such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet’s Google will not be affected.
Have tech firms been abusing US immigration rules?
Critics of the H-1B visa and PERM green card process argue that some employers use the system not to fill legitimate skills shortages, but to reduce labour costs, gain leverage over workers and make it harder for US employees to compete for jobs. They say companies do this by hiring foreign workers at lower wages and manipulating recruitment conditions to keep out qualified US workers.
Vance said Microsoft last year let go 6,000 US workers, while also securing 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vance.
Sonderling said companies being suspended from PERM had received more than 230,000 H-1B visas and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications since 2009.
“That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.
The H1-B visa system has also emerged as a lightning rod for many of the most vocal backers of Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, some of whom have married criticism of the programme with anti-immigrant stereotypes — particularly against Indians — to demand that the scheme be scrapped.
Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented new hires replacing US workers. In a statement, the company said that 80 percent of the roughly 6,000 H1-B visa applications it issued last year were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees”, not for new employees, and that the other filings were for “individuals already legally in the United States”.
The company also said that it only files applications for people who “meet the rigorous standards of this visa category” and that such employees are paid equally to any others who do similar work.
What does this mean for foreign workers?
The suspension could make it harder for foreign workers in the tech industry to obtain permanent residency in the US. Many of those affected are likely to be Indian nationals, who account for a large share of the country’s skilled foreign workforce in the technology sector.
Each year, there are only 85,000 slots for new H-1B visas (not including filings for renewals), but hundreds of thousands of applications. Many H-1B visa holders work in technology-related jobs: 62 percent of the beneficiaries in the 2025 fiscal year worked in computer-related occupations.
Indian nationals account for roughly 70 percent of existing H-1B visa holders.
The Trump administration has already tried to crack down on the H1-B scheme, and in August proposed a new $103,000 fee for H1-B applications, after an earlier pitch for a similar fee was struck down by a federal court. The fee, the government argues, would help provide revenue that could be used to service the vast US immigration system, while reducing the incentive for companies to attempt to misuse H1-B visas.
But the new move to restrict the pathway to a green card for foreign workers already in the US, legally, could impact not just those who might have dreamed of working or living in the US — but thousands already in the country.
The US typically issues around 140,000 employment-based green cards every year. But it also has a strict country-based cap — applicants from any one country cannot receive more than seven percent of green cards issued in a year.
Yet, because the employment-based green card application system is largely used to convert many H1-B visa holders into permanent residents, applicants for permanent residency are disproportionately Indian.
The result: Nearly one million Indians legally in the US on work visas are currently stuck in the employment-based green card backlog. They represent 79 percent of the total green card backlog of around 1.25 million people.
Even before the latest move, Indian green card applicants in certain employment categories would have needed to wait for decades, according to a 2025 analysis for the Congressional Research Service.
Sonderling’s statement that the US will no longer process “any pending permanent labour certification applications” from the blacklisted companies has raised fears that tens of thousands of foreign workers in the country legally — most of them Indian — who have waited for years might suddenly no longer be eligible. For others, the wait could get even longer.
Has India responded?
Yes. India’s Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement saying the US’s suspension does not “advance the shared ambitions of both countries”.
The ministry said that “talent mobility adds value” to both the Indian and US economies, including providing US companies “with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation”.
The ministry also criticised comments by Vance comparing foreign workers to indentured servants as “unwarranted” and “deeply offensive”, saying his words recalled “painful historical and colonial legacy connotations”.
Colonial powers — the British, Dutch and French — took more than 1.6 million Indian workers as indentured labourers to work on plantations and build railways in their other colonies: in Malaysia, Mauritius, South Africa, Kenya, Uganda, Fiji, Suriname, Guyana and other Caribbean countries.
India’s foreign ministry said Vance’s descriptions also “ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem”.
results.summary:
The United States government has suspended major tech companies from the PERM program, halting green card sponsorship for foreign workers to combat alleged visa fraud and labor displacement.

### Key Points
- The Department of Labor will stop processing new and pending permanent labor certification applications for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini.
- Vice President JD Vance accused these firms of using the PERM program to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign staff, citing Microsoft’s recent hiring and layoff data.
- The PERM program is a critical pathway for H-1B visa holders to transition to permanent residency, a process currently backlogged with over 1.2 million applicants.
- Indian nationals, who comprise approximately 70 percent of H-1B visa holders, are expected to be the most significantly impacted by this policy shift.
- India’s Ministry of External Affairs formally criticized the move, labeling Vance’s rhetoric regarding "indentured servants" as offensive and detrimental to bilateral economic cooperation.

### Why it Matters
This policy change creates significant uncertainty for thousands of skilled foreign professionals already residing in the U.S. who now face potential roadblocks to permanent residency. It also signals a more aggressive stance by the administration toward corporate immigration practices, likely forcing major tech firms to re-evaluate their long-term talent acquisition and retention strategies.

results.title: OLED MacBook Pro to help boost premium display shipments, per report
results.author: Marcus Mendes
results.content:
A new Counterpoint Research report says Apple’s next-generation MacBook Pro will help drive a 50% increase in OLED notebook display shipments in 2026 alone. Here are the details.
New MacBook Pro and premium AI PCs expected to fuel demand
In a report released today, Counterpoint Research projects that advanced notebook display shipments will grow 11% in 2026 compared to 2025, with OLED notebook display shipments expected to rise 50% for the period.
The report notes that the 11% growth in advanced notebook display shipments will comfortably outperform the broader notebook display market, which Counterpoint says it expects to decline 3% year over year.
Counterpoint says it also expects OLED to widen its lead over MiniLED in the advanced notebook display market, rising from 56% of shipments in 2025 to 75% in 2026, while MiniLED is expected to drop from 44% to 25%.
The research company says part of the growth in OLED notebook panel shipments is expected to come from Apple’s adoption of the technology in its next-generation MacBook Pro, currently rumored to be announced on October 27 with a touchscreen display and a redesigned, significantly lighter chassis.
Here’s Counterpoint:
OLED notebook display shipments are forecast to rise 50% in 2026 and another 24% in 2027. Apple’s anticipated adoption of OLED in next-generation MacBook Pro models, alongside continued demand for premium AI PCs, is expected to drive this growth.
Another factor contributing to OLED’s growth, Counterpoint says, is technology and manufacturing advances such as tandem OLED architectures, which improve brightness, power efficiency, and panel longevity.
Apple already uses tandem OLED in the iPad Pro, where two OLED layers work together to deliver higher full-screen brightness. The company is widely expected to use a similar two-stack tandem OLED architecture for the upcoming 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models.
Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects OLED notebook panel shipments to grow at a compounded annual rate of 26% between 2024 and 2030, while panel revenue is forecast to grow at 35% per year over the same period.
You can read Counterpoint’s full report here.
results.summary:
Apple’s anticipated adoption of OLED technology in upcoming MacBook Pro models is projected to drive a 50% surge in notebook display shipments throughout 2026, according to Counterpoint Research.

### Key Points
- Counterpoint Research forecasts an 11% growth in advanced notebook display shipments for 2026, despite a projected 3% decline in the broader notebook market.
- OLED technology is expected to capture 75% of the advanced notebook display market by 2026, significantly outpacing MiniLED’s projected 25% share.
- Apple is rumored to integrate tandem OLED architecture into new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models to enhance brightness and power efficiency.
- OLED notebook panel shipments are forecast to maintain a 26% compounded annual growth rate through 2030, with annual revenue growth projected at 35%.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward OLED displays signals a major transition in premium hardware standards driven by Apple’s supply chain influence and the rising demand for AI-capable PCs. This trend will likely force competitors to adopt tandem OLED architectures to remain relevant in the high-end laptop market.

results.title: Other Mommy Review: Jessica Chastain Goes Full Pennywise In This Lackluster Horror Movie
results.author: staff@slashfilm.com (Chris Evangelista)
results.content:
Other Mommy Review: Jessica Chastain Goes Full Pennywise In This Lackluster Horror Movie
"Other Mommy" asks a question that we've all pondered from time to time: What if Jessica Chastain was Pennywise the Clown? In this underwhelming but occasionally effective horror movie, Chastain plays a demonic monster just like Stephen King's horrific harlequin. She can shape-shift and alter reality itself, all in the name of a good scare (Chastain, of course, already has a Pennywise connection, having starred in "It: Chapter Two").
Adapted from Josh Malerman's novel "Incidents Around the House" (and let's be honest, "Incidents Around the House" is a much better title than "Other Mommy"), the film helmed by "Host" filmmaker Rob Savage and penned by Nathan Elston, is quite loud and frequently stylish, and Chastain, a consummate professional, is giving it her all as the monster.
But "Other Mommy" feels disjointed and rushed, and worst of all, forgettable. There are hints at something much better, and much more melancholy, beneath it all, but who has time for that when there are jump scares to be had?
Other Mommy could be a lot better
Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark, quite good here as far as child actors go) is a 7-year-old girl living with her frequently absent mother Ursula (Chastain) and her cool stay-at-home dad (or "Daddo," as she annoyingly calls him) Russ (Jay Duplass). "Other Mommy" wastes no time getting to the horror, revealing that Bela keeps being visited by an entity she calls Other Mommy, also played by Chastain. A more predictable route would be for Other Mommy to only be visible to Bela, but "Other Mommy" cleverly subverts expectations and reveals that Bela's parents can see the monster, too.
Other Mommy keeps asking Bela if she can go inside her heart, which clearly can't be a good thing. The monster is bound by rules, however, and she can't achieve her goal unless Bela gives her permission. What she can do, however, is torment Bela and her parents, and anyone else unlucky enough to cross their paths. This leads to one big set piece after another as the family keeps running around trying to escape Other Mommy, only for Other Mommy to show up and wreck havoc and spread death (one of the most memorable moments has her making a character's head explode in slow-motion).
Lurking beneath the horror are domestic issues that, had they been further explored, might have lead to a stronger film. Bela's parents aren't exactly what you'd call "happily married," and Ursula in particular is harboring her share of secrets and resentments. So many movies portray parenthood as a wonderful, joyful thing, and "Other Mommy" is smart enough to suggest that maybe, just maybe, having a kid isn't all it's cracked up to be. I was particularly taken with the last shot, which hints at a kind of deep sadness I wish the film had examined more.
There's some fun to be had with Other Mommy
An VFX-heavy affair, "Other Mommy" unleashes plenty of ghoulish jump scares, with Chastain's Other Mommy altering her appearance in various spooky ways. Savage manages to wring some style out of all of this, especially in the way the film transitions from one scene to the next. But the creature work is never convincing or distinct enough to be scary, and Other Mommy is so consistently violent and monstrous that it makes you wonder why Bela thought she was friendly to begin with.
Still, there's some ghoulish fun to be had here. I particularly enjoyed a moment where the family turns to Ursula's new age mother (Karen Allen!), who brings in some paranormal researchers who prove to be not very helpful when all is said and done. And fans of Chastain will no doubt get a kick out of watching her crawl around on the floor covered in monster makeup while using a creepy voice. But after an admittedly great opening scene (one that's been completely spoiled by the trailers), "Other Mommy" loses its charm. There are much better horror movies you can go see right now.
/Film Rating: 5 out of 10
"Other Mommy" opens in theaters on October 9, 2026.
results.summary:
Jessica Chastain stars as a shape-shifting demonic entity in the horror film Other Mommy, a visually stylish but disjointed adaptation of Josh Malerman’s novel arriving in theaters October 9.

### Key Points
- Directed by Rob Savage and written by Nathan Elston, the film is based on the novel Incidents Around the House.
- Jessica Chastain plays dual roles as both the mother, Ursula, and the titular monster, Other Mommy.
- The cast includes Arabella Olivia Clark as seven-year-old Bela, Jay Duplass as her father, and Karen Allen as her grandmother.
- The plot follows a family attempting to escape a supernatural entity that requires the child's permission to enter her heart.
- The film features heavy visual effects and jump scares, though critics note the creature design lacks distinctiveness.

### Why it Matters
The film highlights a growing trend of adapting contemporary horror novels into high-budget, VFX-heavy studio features. While it explores complex themes of domestic resentment and the challenges of parenthood, its reliance on jump scares over narrative depth may limit its long-term impact on the genre.

results.title: Gas prices are at a record high for October. Iran isn't the only problem.
results.author: Matt Egan, CNN
results.content:
The Strait of Hormuz is no longer paralyzed and yet fuel prices remain painfully high. It’s a vexing problem with profound financial, political and economic consequences.
Gasoline prices, averaging $4.36 a gallon nationally, have never been this high at this time of year, according to AAA data.
Even after a series of emergency steps from US states and Europe, diesel is only about 20 cents away from the all-time high set just last month.
In short, what started as an oil supply crunch caused by the Iran war has morphed into a broader energy crisis being felt by drivers, truckers and farmers around the world.
Unblocking the Strait of Hormuz has been helpful, but it’s still incredibly dangerous – and thus expensive. Not only that, but Russian refineries are getting destroyed by Ukrainian drones, and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea have disrupted a vital shipping lane.
“The wars have not been resolved. There is no peace. The energy system is still constricted,” said Jan Stuart, global energy strategist at Piper Sandler.
‘Insane’ cost of oil supertankers
The security challenges have been underscored by the staggering cost of getting crude oil out of the Middle East.
Last year, the daily cost of hiring an oil supertanker (known as a Very Large Crude Carrier, or VLCC) to sail from the Persian Gulf to China was just $65,000, according to Clarksons, a London-based research firm.
By the time the Iran war was about to begin, that cost had climbed to $230,000 per day.
Now? It costs $1.6 million per day to hire a VLCC for that route, according to Clarksons.
“That’s insane,” said Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser at Gulf Oil. “If you own a tanker, you’re in great shape – as long as it goes unscathed by the war.”
But some tankers are not emerging unscathed.
Multiple commercial vessels reported getting struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz in recent days alone, including at least two crude oil tankers, according to the United Kingdom’s Maritime Trade Operations.
Insurance, sailor costs surge
But it’s not just the cost of hiring a tanker.
It’s the cost of persuading sailors to go on dangerous voyages in war zones.
Some shippers are offering sailors up to $25,000 per trip – an amount that could represent more than a year of wages, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Insurance costs have also skyrocketed, reflecting the risk of sailing through the region with valuable cargo.
Oil producers are now paying between $30 million and $40 million for a round-trip voyage in and out of the Strait of Hormuz, the Journal reported.
Real-world vs. financial price
All of this – the cost to hire a tanker, exorbitant payments to sailors and surging insurance rates – is making it more expensive for consumers and businesses around the world.
It used to cost just $2 per barrel to get crude out of the Persian Gulf. Now, that cost has spiraled to about $33, according to Kloza.
“We’re getting a reasonable amount of crude out, but that’s misleading because the cost of that crude exiting is incredible,” he said.
This helps explain the wide gap between the price of crude in financial markets and the price in the real world.
Consider that the price of Dated Brent – the real-world cost of receiving immediate physical barrels of crude – is $135.74 a barrel as of Thursday, according to S&P Global Platts. That’s well above the Brent futures price of about $100 and not far from the all-time high set in April.
And it’s that real-world price that trickles down to what consumers are paying at the gas station.
“The United States does not live in isolation. We live with a global price because we import gasoline,” said Stuart.
Refineries are getting blown up
The global energy system is not experiencing a single war, but two or arguably three wars – simultaneously.
On top of the US-Iran war, a conflict that has stretched for much longer than many imagined when it started, there is the battle between Yemen and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Houthi drone and missile attacks have disrupted another vital chokepoint for global trade, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
And then there are the increasingly successful Ukrainian drone attacks destroying refineries in Russia, one of the world’s leading exporters of diesel.
Facing fuel shortages at home, Russia has responded by limiting its fuel exports. China, seeking to avoid shortages of its own, has similarly restricted its exports.
US refineries are the only ones left standing. But they are already producing as much gasoline, diesel and jet fuel as they can. Now, some US refineries are dialing back their production for routine maintenance that typically occurs at this time of the year.
Hurricane Isaias could make matters worse if the storm knocks production offline or damages refineries along the US Gulf Coast.
Buffers have vanished
Energy prices would be much, much higher if not for the fact that the world had a sizable rainy day fund built up when the year started.
Commercial and emergency stockpiles act as shock absorbers during crises.
But now those inventories have been aggressively drawn down, leaving the world with less margin for error now. Those shrinking stockpiles have driven up the premium built into current prices.
“We are running on very, very low inventories. We don’t have buffers anymore,” said Stuart.
All of this explains why prices remain high and the risks are elevated – even as the flow of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz has recovered towards pre-war levels.
“You have to end all three wars – or even two out of three wouldn’t be bad,” said Kloza.
results.summary:
Global fuel prices remain at record highs as geopolitical conflicts and surging shipping costs create a persistent energy crisis despite the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

### Key Points
- Daily costs to hire oil supertankers have surged to $1.6 million, up from $65,000 last year.
- Real-world crude prices, represented by Dated Brent, have reached $135.74 per barrel, significantly outpacing futures markets.
- Shipping companies are paying sailors up to $25,000 per trip to navigate dangerous war zones.
- Global supply is constrained by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries.
- Commercial and emergency oil stockpiles have been depleted, leaving the global market with no remaining buffers against further supply shocks.

### Why it Matters
The disconnect between financial oil markets and real-world delivery costs is driving sustained inflation for consumers and businesses globally. As energy inventories hit critical lows, the global economy remains highly vulnerable to further supply chain disruptions or extreme weather events.
